newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, buyers stay sidelined.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, buyers stay sidelined.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended lower on Thursday as sidelined buyers let prices slowly erode throughout the session.

Participants said next week's busy calendar of significant economic data, remarks by Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer and the substantial new supply auctioned this week combined to pressure prices of U.S. government securities.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 93-27/32, down 15/32, to yield 7.13 percent. Two-year notes slipped 3/32 to 99-23/32, ending with a 6.53 percent yield.

E. Craig Coats, manager of government securities trading at Prudential Securities Inc., said the sticking point for the Treasury market on Thursday and earlier this week was the lack of retail demand for U.S. fixed-income securities.

"Wall Street bought the two-year and the five-year and there's really no followthrough retail demand," said Coats, referring to the Treasury auctions this week of $17.0 billion in two-year notes and $12.5 billion in five-year notes.
Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets, agreed.

"You have a fairly identifiable trend this week," said Karydakis. "Everytime the market goes up, there's a complete lack of followthrough. That sets the market back a little bit and you go back to square one."
Karydakis said it was understandable that retail buyers would make themselves scarce "given what happens next week with that crowded economic calendar."
Next week brings a powerful group of economic data.
The first-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), said to be favored by Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, is due on Tuesday. The first-quarter real GDP number is due a day later.
The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) April survey is due on May 1 and April U.S. employment data are due on May 2.
"The natural inclination of participants is to stand on the sidelines and hold their ammunition until next week," Karydakis said.
A speech by Fed Governor Laurence Meyer to the Forecasters Club in New York on Thursday also came in as a negative for the bond market, participants said.

At a question-and-answer session that was closed to the press, Meyer said Fed monetary policy in 1996 was not as restrictive as some U.S. policymakers thought at the time, sources told Reuters. He said incoming early 1997 that "created a collection of stories .. that suggested above-trend growth" had persuaded him to vote for the Fed's 25-basis-point hike in the Federal funds rate on March 25. As other Fed officials have done, Meyer acknowledged that tight labor markets were a key concern for the Fed.
"The Meyer comments were viewed as the comments of someone who was leaning toward more tightening," said Karydakis.
The Meyer speech was clear, said Coats. "This is not a positive environment for fixed-income securities."

Coats said the Fed is likely to raise interest rates by at least another 25 basis points at its May policy meeting. And he said that if the Employment Cost Index (ECI) due next week is up more than one percent, "people will start to talk about the Fed being behind the curve (on fighting inflation)."

Augmenting fixed-income supply on Thursday were some new corporate debt offerings. A Comcast Corp unit deal was upped to $1.7 billion from an initially planned sale of $1.0 billion, market sources said. And Banc One sold $900 million in subordinated debt.
The Treasury also sold $13.75 billion in 52-week notes at an average yield of 5.72 percent.

"The Treasury auction was fine," said Coats. "It came and went. One-year bills are a professional piece of paper anyway. They're not a bad place to hide out if you're uncertain about other fixed-income securities or even equities."
Though Treasury prices ended lower, prices remained within recent boundaries.
"The market didn't really get killed," said Coats.
"Trading still is on the very light side," said Karydakis. "People are marking time until they see next week's data."
Three-month bill rates fell three basis points to 5.16 percent. Six-month bill rates rose three basis points to 5.38 percent.
Year bill rates rose two basis points to 5.66 percent.
Five-year notes fell 7/32 to 99-5/32, yielding 6.83 percent.
The 6-1/4 percent 10-year notes ended down 10/32 to 95-8/32, yielding 6.92 percent.
